claims.statement: URE reported 1,544,574 grid-connected RES microinstallations in Poland at the end of 2024, with 99.7% of exported microinstallation energy coming from PV and more than 98% of installations owned by prosumers; this establishes a large broad PV stock but not the count of commercial systems whose exact inverter model, age, support status, and downtime criticality qualify for this reserve.

IEA PVPS describes inverter technical life as roughly 10-15 years and reports that about 10% of inverters in a monitored sample of roughly 2,000 commercial PV plants had been replaced by year six, with the observed replacement rate falling from above 4% in year one to below 1% in year five; these international figures do not establish failure incidence for the proposed Polish cohorts.

IEA PVPS identifies inverter failure as a material source of lost revenue and recommends that EPC/O&M contracts specify replacement procedures, cost allocation, reaction and repair times, and quantified non-production losses, supporting downtime as a measurable loss and availability as a contractible concern.

IEA PVPS states that production losses while supply-chain parties dispute or wait for delivery can exceed the value of an O&M contract and can be reduced with a planned spare-parts list and replacement inverters, which also shows that an owner, EPC, or O&M contractor can internalize the proposed reserve through ordinary stocking provisions.

NREL's 2024 workshop report records a refurbishment case with a 0.9-year return on investment versus 2.7-3.3 years for new-inverter solutions, string-inverter swaps within hours, and central-inverter replacement costs up to USD 500,000 including logistics and labor; the report simultaneously says payback is project-specific and ultimately depends on labor and site logistics.

NREL's workshop participants reported that its cost benchmark did not include warranties and lead times and that suppliers were typically selected on performance or cost rather than spare-parts lead time, which is contrary evidence against assuming a standalone availability fee will be a purchasing priority without account-level validation.

SolarEdge's Poland offer sells a one-time protection extension purchased within 24 months of shipment and says an eligible replacement unit is generally shipped within 48 hours, providing a direct OEM substitute for the proposed recurring reservation on supported equipment.

SolarEdge's EU price list quotes total 20-year inverter warranty extensions at EUR 347 for a three-phase inverter below 15 kW, EUR 396 for 25-40 kW, EUR 699 for 50-66.6 kW, and EUR 1,049 for 82.8-100 kW; these one-time OEM prices are a material willingness-to-pay benchmark, although they apply only to eligible SolarEdge equipment rather than already-unsupported legacy units.

SolarEdge lists multiple authorized distributors in Poland and warns that buying from an unauthorized seller can remove limited-warranty coverage and restrict service and support, showing that provenance and authorized-channel status materially affect a replacement unit's value.

SMA says it normally sends a comparable updated replacement device within 48 hours after an order, routes owners through installers, and can supply a current-product repowering device instead, demonstrating an incumbent replacement pool and an established installer service channel.

SMA's repowering guide confirms that discontinued legacy spares and long lead times can cause long downtime, but it also supplies a cross-brand repowering route and requires engineering checks of MPP voltage/current, short-circuit current, AC output, transformer conditions, local installation requirements, and other site parameters before replacement.

PTPiREE's DSO procedure makes compliant certification mandatory under its stage-II process from 1 January 2027 and says a DSO can still refuse connection where current technical requirements are unmet, so a physical fit or model label alone is insufficient evidence of lawful grid compatibility.

A May 2025 Polish buyer contract specification requires paid service during the warranty period, annual PV checks, inverter diagnostics every five years, parts delivery as needed, manufacturer-funded warranty spares, separately paid consumables, and action within four working days after a defect report; this is direct buyer evidence for maintenance and parts obligations, not for a prepaid pooled reservation.

A Polish public buyer awarded a PLN 358,000 lot to replace existing grid inverters with new hybrid inverters and add batteries across operating PV sites, with a 20-day delivery term and price/warranty evaluation criteria; because the lot bundles multiple inverters, storage, and installation, it proves a paid modernization event but not a legacy-reserve price or margin.

The combined evidence supports a real budget and urgency for some inverter maintenance, replacement, and modernization events, but it does not show that buyers prefer an annual third-party reserve over warranties, ordinary O&M spares, repair, or planned repowering.

Installers and authorized distributors are plausible distribution origins because OEM service processes route owners through installers and recognized channels, but no evidence establishes this candidate's acquisition cost, conversion rate, customer-relationship control, or signed channel access.

No evidence establishes the regional qualifying-account denominator by exact inverter model, serial cohort, commissioning year, remaining warranty, OEM support state, site criticality, and current replacement lead time.
No paid reservation, signed letter of intent, price test, renewal, replenishment order, or repeat purchase for the proposed 300-1,200 PLN annual availability product is evidenced.

No candidate-owned inventory, exclusive or durable supply agreement, protected stock allocation, purchase option, supplier warranty, minimum-yield commitment, or enforceable replenishment term is evidenced for any named legacy cohort.

Fully loaded unit economics remain unknown because no cohort-level evidence quantifies acquisition and failure yield, testing labor, storage, insurance, financing, channel share, dispatch, warranty returns, misdiagnosis, refurbishment loss, obsolescence write-downs, disposal, taxes, or support overhead against contracted revenue.

A useful model-level stocking forecast would require longitudinal failures plus configuration, firmware, environment, repair outcome, and exposure data rather than an installed-base census alone; this follows from IEA's identified data-quality gaps and NREL's requirement for at least three years of granular system data in its fleet initiative.

No evidence shows that this candidate can obtain the necessary longitudinal data, that its forecasts improve stocking or swap decisions beyond OEM/O&M tools, or that such improvement causes repeat paid orders.

OEM rapid replacement, paid extended warranties, owner/O&M self-stocking, and current-model cross-brand repowering make the proposed reserve reproducible by incumbents through service or stocking agreements; any defensible gap would therefore have to be demonstrated within narrowly unsupported cohorts rather than assumed across the installed base.
No signed commitment or allocated liability is evidenced from a qualified electrician, testing laboratory, logistics provider, refurbisher, recycler, insurer, O&M channel, or fleet owner.

No tested interchangeability matrix or field validation establishes that different sites can safely pool named inverter, board, adapter, firmware, topology, and grid-code combinations under one service promise.
No public evidence quantifies current Polish stockout frequency, unsupported-model RMA lead time, emergency sourcing cost, repair refusal rate, or downtime loss for any proposed equipment cohort.

The legal classification, conformity documentation, warranty status, product-liability coverage, test protocol, and waste-versus-reusable status of acquired legacy units have not been established for this operating model.

contrary_evidence: SolarEdge and SMA publicly describe OEM replacement-device processes that generally ship eligible replacements within 48 hours, directly compressing the service gap for supported products.
SolarEdge sells one-time long warranty extensions at published euro prices, creating a lower-frequency incumbent alternative to an annual third-party reservation for eligible equipment.

SMA offers engineered cross-brand repowering and Polish public procurement shows buyers paying to replace existing inverters with current hybrid equipment, so modernization can dominate like-for-like legacy stocking.

IEA PVPS explicitly recommends planned spare lists and replacement inverters within ordinary owner/EPC/O&M practice, making the reserve reproducible through a stocking clause rather than a unique control point.
SolarEdge warns that unauthorized supply can lose warranty and support, weakening the commercial value of inventory obtained without protected authorized-channel provenance.
NREL workshop evidence says supplier choice is commonly driven by performance and cost rather than spare lead time, and its economic examples are highly site- and labor-dependent.

Observed international commercial-inverter replacements were concentrated in early life and fell below 1% annually by year five in the IEA PVPS sample, which may limit repeat dispatch revenue absent a precisely selected aging cohort.

Polish certification and current DSO technical requirements constrain substitutions, while SMA's guide shows that electrical, firmware, transformer, and site characteristics fragment compatibility pools.
